tn.quote: § 2. — Accent et ton. Accent comme celui de l'AJIË. Tous les phonèmes sont très nasalisés. Tons analogues à ceux de l'AJIË et du BOEWE. ... Deux syllabes ayant la même consonne et la même voyelle peuvent se distinguer par une différence de hauteur musicale. En indiquant par l'indice 1 le ton le plus bas, on note aisément quatre tons différents. xere¹ = nous, est bas; xere³ = eux, est haut. tn.translation: § 2. Accent and tone. Accent like that of Ajië. All the phonemes are strongly nasalised. Tones analogous to those of Ajië and Boewe. ... Two syllables with the same consonant and the same vowel can be distinguished by a difference in musical pitch. Marking the lowest tone with index 1, one easily notes four different tones. xere¹ = we, is low; xere³ = they, is high. Differences of musical pitch moreover distinguish many monosyllabic full words: ko¹ spirit, ko² cloud, ko³ be ashamed ... ka⁴ laugh

3349.prule: No stress rule is stated anywhere in the source: a 52-word explorer's list taken down on the Juruá in 1867, with a one-sentence orthographic note and no phonological remark beyond f/h. Observation only, not a statement by the author: 50 of the 52 entries carry an acute on the final vowel (unaccented: Afina, Isama; an extra non-final acute: Amóa-huá; an acute on both vowels: Wáú). The note says the spelling follows Portuguese as adopted in Martius's Glossaria, whose acute (Martius 1863: 29) marks a stressed syllable, a 'sharpened' vowel, or two vowels in hiatus; Wáú, Naida-á and Hina-á show the non-stress uses inside this very list, and the acutes on final -í/-ú (Awí, Atú, Chirí, Jujú, Mahí, Carú, Fazú...) are redundant as Portuguese stress marks (final -i/-u is oxytone by default), so they are either positive prominence marks or Martius's vowel-sharpening - undecidable from the page. the compilation 'fixed-final' (confidence low) is an inference from a transcriber's diacritics, not a described stress system, and does not meet the fixed and quantity-insensitive bar of our rule 8 (a stated, quantity-insensitive, word-level position).

3350.dloc: p. 19, section 'Accentos e syllabas'; wordlist p. 21 (image) for the accent-marked forms.
3350.prule: No positional rule is stated. Penna's section is a transcription convention: the acute accent is written over the 'syllaba dominante' (stressed syllable) of each word, the other syllables being short or semi-long (grave/circumflex = semi-long); when a word carries no acute, the dominant syllable is the one containing 'u allemão' ([ü]) or a diphthong; unaccented final syllables are always short. Stress is thus recorded item by item across the 224-item list. My own check of the list page p. 21 (image): acute-marked forms are mostly penultimate (camucáua, eytána, yçahále, p'kyáua, púdy, lápu, kuáke, reáte, yuáte, mamíke, p'ducanúku, p'púye, ucatáca, yuády), a few final (p'partán, caláy, tepáuctekúy), two double-marked (álamáy, tepáuctekúy), and many forms carry no acute at all (malèy, ôrapay, totôre, p'camissa, sòo, fayny, p'çapeua, dykiche, duny, catamare). That tally is a compiler's count, not the source's claim; the source itself does not generalise.
3350.srule: Not mentioned in Ferreira Penna 1881 (pp. 18-19 'Notas sobre a pronunciação' and 'Accentos e syllabas'; wordlist pp. 21-25): only one 'syllaba dominante' per word is described. A few list forms are printed with two acutes (álamáy 'paneiro', tepáuctekúy 'igreja', p. 21) without comment.
3350.quote: Para representar com clareza as flexões das palavras, eu emprego, não só os dous accentos mais usados, mas tambem o grave ou inclinado. O accento agudo é sempre sobre-posto à syllaba dominante, sendo as outras breves ou semi-longas; semi-longas serão as que tiverem accento grave ou circumflexo. Quando a palavra não tiver accento agudo, a syllaba dominante será aquella em que se achar o u allemão ou um diphtongo. As syllabas terminaes, em cuja vogal não ha accento, são sempre breves.

3354.cfw: Dirks 1953 (as quoted in Crothers, Lorentz, Sherman & Vihman 1979) reports one stress per word that tends to the penult with unexplained exceptions and is probably phonemic, whereas Pike & Kindberg 1956, the only study devoted to Campa stress, describe up to five primary stresses per word whose distribution behaves like high tone, a system Goedemans, Heinz & van der Hulst 2015 could only encode as no metrical stress and Hyman 1977 proposed reanalysing with secondary stresses, so the two first-hand descriptions agree only that stress is not rule-governed and no later work on Asháninka settles what kind of system it is.

evidence_works.detail: Comparative sketch and wordlists of five Ambon 'bahasa tanah' dialects by the colonial controleur, with Asilulu (Asilœlœ, the negori-ampat dialect of Seit, Lima, Oering and Asilœlœ, p. 11) as one of the five. His marking convention is stated: stress falls as a rule on the penultimate syllable 'as is frequently the case in Malay', but in the dialects of Haruku and Asilulu it 'verspringt... meermalen, en dikwijls op zeer grillige wijze' (shifts repeatedly, often very capriciously); where it does, the sign (') over the syllable shows where the stress must fall; and the vowel of the stressed syllable is as a rule pronounced long (pp. 13-14). His p. This agrees with the entry's coding (penultimate rule, lexically marked exceptions, suffixes and clitics leaving the root's stress in place, Collins 1983 p. 82 and Collins 2003 p. xxviii). The entry's cfw already carries his remark that Asilulu shifts stress more often than its neighbours; what the work adds beyond the cfw is his statement that the vowel of the stressed syllable is as a rule pronounced long (p. 14), his p. 11 remark that on Haruku the Muslim villages differ from the Christian ones only in stress placement, and the p. 12 accented forms.

3360.prule: Stress is contrastive (lexical). Jijón y Caamaño (as reported by Gómez Rendón) state that most Esmeraldeño words carry the prosodic accent on the penultimate syllable, and that Pallares' accent marks on paroxytone words, written when the norm would be not to, appear to be used contrastively; Adelaar reads the frequent accent diacritics in Seler's edition of the same corpus as suggesting that stress was contrastive. Penult is the majority position, not a rule.

3362.dq: In absolute final position, short vowels are usually deleted in polysyllabic words; e.g., /amiskwa/, amiskw 'beaver'. Exceptions are found, however, and not only in monosyllabic words; when occuring in this position, short vowels usually receive a secondary stress.
3362.prule: Not stated. Béland distinguishes stressed from 'weak (unstressed)' syllables (short vowels centralise in the latter) and gives a secondary stress to short vowels kept in absolute word-final position, but nowhere says where primary word stress falls; Cooper 1945 only remarks that final diphthongs show 'fairly balanced stress' between their two elements. No placement rule can be read off either source.
3362.srule: A short vowel exceptionally retained in absolute word-final position (niska 'goose', maskwa 'bear', mikko 'blood', otehi 'heart'; final short vowels are otherwise usually deleted in polysyllables) 'usually receive[s] a secondary stress'. No other secondary or rhythmic stresses are described; primary-stress placement is not stated, so the relation of this secondary stress to the main stress is unknown.
3362.quote: Short /i/, /a/ and /o/ are subject to a certain number of phonemic rules that sometimes neutralize completely their vowel quality. In weak (unstressed) syllables, short vowels are indiscriminantely centralized to -ʌ- or -ə-; e.g., the vowels /o/ in a:šokan 'bridge, pier, wharf' and /i/ in ašikan 'stockings' are phonetically identical. Exceptions are found, however, and not only in monosyllabic words; when occuring in this position, short vowels usually receive a secondary stress. E.g., niska 'goose'; maskwa 'bear'; mikko 'blood'; otehi 'heart'. The short final vowels /i/ and /a/ are kept in many particles; e.g., ekoši 'let's go'; ni:šitana 'twenty'.
